members.name: Karthick N A
members.contribution: Application architecture, FastAPI backend and Streamlit interface integration; local runtime setup and end-to-end workflow validation.

situated_learning.anchor: I selected an e-commerce customer-support workflow as an industry analogue for applying RetailAssist. In this scenario, DemoMart support agents handle questions about orders, delivery, payments, refunds and account access. The workflow starts with reading a customer message, identifying its topic, checking the applicable policy and preparing a reply. Repeating these steps manually can lead to inconsistent categorisation and unnecessary policy-search effort. I focused on assisting the agent with these activities while retaining human approval of the final response. I used public customer-service data and representative store policies and tickets, avoiding the need to expose confidential workplace records. The expected benefit is more consistent triage and easier access to policy evidence; a reduction in handling time would need to be established through a timed workplace pilot.
situated_learning.apply:
I adapted the application around an agent-facing workflow, connecting the Streamlit interface to FastAPI endpoints for ticket analysis and policy questions. The locally fine-tuned DistilBERT model predicts one of 27 customer-service intents. A separate sentiment model identifies negative, neutral or positive tone, and Qwen summarises the customer's issue. The RAG component searches eight policy PDFs using MiniLM embeddings and supplies the relevant passages to Qwen for a cited response.

For the refund-delay example, the customer states that the returned item was received and inspected nine business days earlier but the refund has not arrived. The workspace identifies a refund-tracking intent and negative sentiment, and the summary retains the delay and its timing reference. The retrieved returns-and-refunds policy explains the 5–7 business-day period after receipt and inspection and the escalation step when a refund remains missing. The response explicitly states that live customer, order and payment records are unavailable, so a support agent must verify the particular refund status. The draft remains editable before use.

I also examined the recorded delivery-period and password-recovery cases. These connect the intent predictions to practical guidance: standard delivery takes 3–5 business days after dispatch, while password recovery uses the Forgot password email flow. The policy chatbot supports follow-up questions and declines a warranty question that the documents do not cover. The application screenshots and recorded predictions provide evidence of these inputs, outputs and source references.
situated_learning.analyse:
I evaluated workplace relevance by separating performance on the public dataset from performance on independently prepared tickets. The fine-tuned intent classifier achieved public-test macro-F1 of 0.998, compared with 0.988 for the TF-IDF baseline. Its macro-F1 fell to 0.688 on 81 independent evaluation tickets. This gap shows that success on the source dataset does not establish equivalent reliability on different customer phrasing. The near-template audit found 138 close training matches among 500 sampled public-test messages, which helps explain why the public score needs caution. Some incorrect predictions also had high confidence, so an agent should review the predicted intent rather than treat confidence as certainty.

Sentiment macro-F1 was 0.975 on the same ticket set. Retrieval Recall@4 was 100% across 20 answerable policy questions, and all five unsupported questions were declined. Retrieval coverage and valid source identifiers do not establish that every answer is semantically correct; expert review remains important. I interpret these results as evidence of a useful prototype with clear generalisation limits. Workflow efficiency still requires paired human timing, and production concurrency, authentication and live CRM integration have not been demonstrated.
situated_learning.reflect:
Before workplace deployment, I would address customer-data access, authentication, retention and deletion, policy ownership and integration with the organisation's support systems. Account and payment information would require appropriate access controls and review against organisational and applicable data-protection requirements. Local inference avoids paid model-usage fees, but hardware capacity, response time, maintenance and concurrent usage still have a cost. The prototype can explain policies and prepare drafts; it cannot execute refunds, change orders or verify customer records. Recognised claims of completed business actions are rejected, but that safeguard is not a complete defence against prompt manipulation.

The single most important improvement I would prioritise is validation and calibration on representative, expert-reviewed workplace tickets and policy answers. The drop from 0.998 public-test macro-F1 to 0.688 on independent tickets provides a concrete reason to prioritise this work. A reviewed, anonymised dataset and a stable held-out test set would expose the actual error patterns and guide model adaptation and escalation thresholds before broader integration. My conclusion is that RetailAssist should initially support an agent's judgement, with transaction decisions and outgoing responses remaining under human control.

members.name: Ramya T
members.contribution: Dataset preparation and reproducible train/validation/test splits; TF-IDF baseline, DistilBERT fine-tuning and intent-classification evaluation.

situated_learning.anchor: I focused on the problem of assigning customer messages to the right support category. In an e-commerce support team, requests about cancellations, invoices, delivery and refunds can look similar even though they need different next steps. A routing mistake can lead to another handoff or an irrelevant reply. I used DemoMart as an industry analogue to examine this problem without using confidential customer records. My aim was to see whether a small, locally fine-tuned model could give an agent a useful starting point for triage. I treated the prediction as a recommendation that the agent should check, particularly when a message contains several issues or uses unfamiliar wording.
situated_learning.apply:
My main area of contribution was preparing the intent-classification data and assessing the fine-tuned model. We used the customer instruction from the Bitext dataset as the input and its intent as the target. The supplied response and category were excluded from the model inputs. After normalisation and deduplication, the data contained 24,274 examples, split into 19,419 training, 2,427 validation and 2,428 test examples. We compared a TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline with DistilBERT, fine-tuned for three epochs, and selected the checkpoint using validation macro-F1.

In the application, this saved classifier is part of a wider support workflow. It identifies the likely topic, the sentiment model helps the agent understand tone, Qwen condenses the message, and the policy chatbot retrieves relevant guidance from the store documents. For example, a message asking about an approved refund that has not reached the customer's bank is classified as refund tracking. The associated policy answer explains the refund timeline and when to contact support. A delivery-period question leads to the standard shipping estimate, while a password-recovery question leads to the account-recovery procedure.

These examples show how classification can support the next step, but the final reply also needs the policy evidence and the original customer message. The interface keeps the reply editable and makes clear that the prototype cannot inspect live customer records or perform transactions.
situated_learning.analyse:
The public-test results initially looked very strong: the fine-tuned classifier achieved macro-F1 of 0.998, compared with 0.988 for the baseline. The independent set of 81 tickets gave a more demanding result, with intent macro-F1 of 0.688. I consider that difference the most important finding from the classification evaluation. The source dataset contains related templates, and the audit found 138 close training matches in a sample of 500 public-test messages. Removing exact duplicates therefore did not remove every source of similarity between the splits.

A recorded error illustrates the practical risk. A customer questioning the tax figure on an invoice was assigned to refund tracking with a confidence score of about 0.978. The high score would not make that routing decision useful to a support agent. I would assess the model by its errors across support categories and its ability to handle new phrasing, alongside the aggregate score. The sentiment and retrieval components add useful context, but they do not correct every intent error. The prototype has demonstrated the workflow; it has not established reliable unattended triage or a measured reduction in handling time.
situated_learning.reflect:
My priority before deployment would be to validate the intent model on representative, expert-labelled workplace tickets. That is the single improvement I would put first because the independent-ticket result shows a substantial gap between the source benchmark and new customer wording. The workplace set should cover short messages, mixed issues, informal language and distinctions such as refund eligibility versus refund progress. A stable held-out set would then support per-category evaluation and decisions about when an agent should take over.

Collecting that data would also require anonymisation, controlled access and an appropriate retention policy. I would retain model and dataset versions so that changes could be investigated, and I would check the organisation's data-protection requirements before using real tickets. Local execution avoids a paid inference service, but training, maintenance and concurrent requests still use hardware resources. Until the workplace validation supports a broader role, I would keep the classifier as an aid to the agent and preserve human responsibility for routing and outgoing responses.

members.name: Arthi S S
members.contribution: Synthetic store-policy authoring, PDF knowledge-base preparation, embedding and retrieval pipeline, and grounded policy-chatbot development.

situated_learning.anchor: I examined the policy-lookup part of an e-commerce support workflow. An agent may need to find a return window, a cancellation condition or a delivery estimate while also understanding the customer's particular concern. When that information is spread across documents, there is a risk of using an incomplete passage or relying on a remembered rule. I used DemoMart as a retail industry analogue and concentrated on making the policy evidence easy to retrieve and check. The intended benefit is a more traceable and consistent reply, with the agent able to see the document behind it.
situated_learning.apply:
My focus was the knowledge base and the retrieval-augmented chatbot. We prepared eight policy documents covering orders, delivery, refunds, payments, accounts, support, promotions and agent procedures. The 24 PDF pages form the retrieval source. We indexed the PDFs once, keeping document names, sections and page references, and divided their text into 180-token windows with 30-token overlap. MiniLM produced normalised 384-dimensional embeddings, stored in a local NumPy index. For a question, the backend retrieves four passages by cosine similarity and passes the relevant evidence to Qwen.

The other tasks contribute to the same workflow. The fine-tuned DistilBERT model suggests the ticket's intent, sentiment analysis identifies tone, and the summary helps the agent review the customer's issue. The chatbot then provides policy guidance with references that the agent can expand. In the recorded cancellation example, it explains that an order cannot be cancelled after dispatch and that the return process may be available after delivery. In the refund example, it cites the 5–7 business-day period after receipt and inspection. It declines a five-year warranty question because that policy is absent from the documents.

I treated the source reference as an essential part of the answer. The backend places a reference beside each answer statement, checks its evidence quotation and selected policy qualifications, and discloses the lack of live customer-record access. This keeps a policy explanation separate from a claim that an order or refund has actually been checked.
situated_learning.analyse:
Retrieval Recall@4 was 100% for the 20 answerable policy questions: the expected document was among the four retrieved passages in every case. All five unsupported questions were declined. The automatic fact-keyword check passed for {rag_keyword_passes} of the 20 answerable questions. I would not read those figures as proof that every answer is correct. Recall measures whether the source was retrieved, and a keyword check can miss a valid paraphrase or accept an answer that needs more careful review.

The current corpus is small and internally consistent, which makes the demonstration manageable but limits what it establishes about a workplace knowledge base. Real support documents can contain exceptions, old versions and overlapping rules. The intent model's drop from 0.998 public-test macro-F1 to 0.688 on independent tickets also reinforces the need to check the full workflow rather than assume that one strong component makes the whole response reliable. The recorded adversarial refund case showed a further risk: a model can make an unsupported claim of action despite citing a policy. The final guard rejects recognised action claims, while agent review remains necessary.
situated_learning.reflect:
The single improvement I would prioritise is a controlled knowledge base of current, owner-approved workplace policies. Each document should have a responsible owner, an effective date and a clear process for replacing an obsolete version. I would put this first for the retrieval component because a well-written answer can still be wrong if it is grounded in an outdated or incomplete policy. A broader set of representative questions should be checked against those approved documents before deployment.

Workplace integration would also require access controls for internal documents, protection of customer information and retention rules consistent with the organisation's obligations. The assistant should not expose restricted passages to an unauthorised user. Local models reduce reliance on an external inference service, but indexing, response time, monitoring and maintenance still need support. I would retain the read-only, agent-reviewed workflow until the organisation has verified the knowledge sources and any connection to its order or customer-service systems.

members.name: Renukadevi T
members.contribution: Sentiment and summarization workflow validation; evaluation evidence, application screenshots, report preparation and demonstration coordination.

situated_learning.anchor: I focused on the quality of the reply that a customer receives. In a support workflow, a message may be long, frustrated or unclear, and an agent needs to identify the essential facts before choosing an appropriate response. A concise reply is useful only if it retains the customer's issue, follows the policy and sets a realistic expectation. I used the DemoMart industry analogue to examine how sentiment, summarisation and retrieved evidence could support that judgement. My aim was to help the agent prepare a clear response while keeping approval and escalation under human control.
situated_learning.apply:
I considered the four tasks as a connected communication workflow. The locally fine-tuned DistilBERT model identifies the likely support intent. RoBERTa estimates whether the message is negative, neutral or positive, and Qwen summarises the issue. The RAG chatbot then uses the store's eight policy PDFs to prepare a response with source references. The agent can inspect those references and edit the draft before using it.

The refund-delay example makes the purpose of these steps clear. The customer says the returned item was received and inspected nine business days earlier, but the money has not arrived. The workspace identifies refund tracking and negative sentiment. The summary preserves the timing and the inspection event, which matters because the policy's refund period starts after receipt and inspection. The reply explains the 5–7 business-day period and the support escalation step, while stating that the prototype cannot check live records.

I also used the recorded cancellation summary as an example of fact retention: it keeps the customer's mistaken purchase, distress and request to stop the item before shipment. Delivery and password-recovery questions provide additional examples of procedural guidance. These cases allow the agent to check tone, completeness and policy support rather than judging the response only by how fluent it sounds.
situated_learning.analyse:
Sentiment macro-F1 was 0.975 on the 81 independently prepared tickets. That result is encouraging for the demonstration, but the examples contain relatively clear sentiment cues and have not been independently labelled by a second reviewer. Mixed messages can combine appreciation with a complaint, so sentiment should inform the agent's reading rather than determine urgency or entitlement by itself. The intent model's macro-F1 of 0.688 on independent tickets also shows why an agent should check the topic before acting on a confident prediction.

For policy answers, Recall@4 was 100% on 20 answerable questions and the automatic keyword pass rate was {rag_keyword_percent}. An earlier evaluation illustrates the keyword check's limitation with the promotional-code answer: it correctly says that a code cannot be added after confirming an order, while the expected keyword uses a different form of that wording. Surface checks therefore need interpretation. Mean response time for the evaluated RAG requests was about {rag_mean_seconds} seconds; this is a model-request measurement, not an end-to-end measure of an agent's handling time. The prototype has not yet established a human productivity gain or performance under concurrent workplace use.
situated_learning.reflect:
My first priority would be an agent-reviewed workplace pilot that checks summary faithfulness and policy accuracy on representative tickets. I would make that the single most important improvement because the final response is what the customer sees, and an omitted timing condition or an unsupported promise could be consequential even when the wording is polite. The pilot should record whether the summary retains the necessary facts, whether each policy claim is supported, and whether the agent needs to correct or escalate the response. Paired manual and assisted tasks could then measure time to an approved reply.

The pilot would need anonymised inputs, controlled access, suitable record-retention rules and review against organisational data-protection requirements. Verified CRM integration would be needed before the system could show actual order or refund status. Local inference avoids usage-based model fees, but hardware capacity, maintenance and peak-load response time still matter. I would keep a human agent responsible for the final message and any business action, using the model outputs as supporting information.
